title: Trump Announces New “AI Force”
author: Ken Klippenstein

While the media fixates on AI extinction scenarios, government and industry
are fighting over something far more concrete: who gets to control America's
response to AI.

"I am forming the AI Force, much like I did [the] Space Force," Donald Trump
[said](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117298821562014906) last
Saturday.

Almost immediately, the AI shark tank started circling, eager to shape the
president's musings into something concrete, something that would benefit --
them.

It's a Washington playbook and a kind of Rorschach test: the movers and
shakers, the experts and the moguls telling you what the president "meant,"
what an AI Force should be, whether it's needed, and if it's not, what's
needed instead. It's a trillion-dollar Christmas wishlist you're paying for
but have no say in the contents, which will dictate the future of AI.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2H5z!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-

AI Force announcement

A seventh military branch, alongside the Air Force, Army, Coast Guard, Marine
Corps, Navy, and Space? Another military command alongside Cyber Command or
Strategic Command? Another powerful agency like NSA?

Trump's Space Force comparison is "the shape of an answer, but without the
substance," Philip Reiner, CEO and co-founder of the Institute for Security
and Technology, [told](https://www.defenseone.com/policy/2026/09/trump-ai-
force/416125/) Defense One. Everyone is rushing in to fill that empty vessel.

"Space Force works because Congress can give it a doctrine, a budget, a
personnel system, but there's no equivalent for AI," Reiner said, adding:
"this is more of an actual [Defense Department] lane…"

Then there's Leah Siskind of the hawkish Foundation for Defense of
Democracies, who said that she sees Trump's AI Force as "a key vehicle for
bolstering artificial intelligence expertise across the Defense Department and
the rest of the federal government."

Of course the naysayers point to impediments like the need for new laws, a
budget, and an act of Congress, yadda yadda, but that's not how things
congeal. Quickly the consensus has formed that some kind of military entity
needs to take over.

Congressman Rich McCormick (R-GA), a member of the Armed Services Committee
and former Navy commander, embraced Trump's idea.

"President Trump's proposal for an AI Force Czar puts a needed focus on
accelerating American innovation and cutting through barriers that slow us
down," McCormick said. "China is moving fast. America needs to move faster."

Okay, he says Czar, which suggests civilian rather than military, but the
national security red card has been flashed: that because of China, we need to
do something big. Before you know it, Washington has declared an AI war.

At least one tech industry figure expressed misgivings, noting that the Space
Force comparison portends a military takeover of the tech sector.

"Rather than use civilian agencies to regulate it, use the Pentagon to try and
dominate it," an industry representative
[told](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/19/tech-industry-scratches-head-
over-ai-force-01085319) _Politico_.

One person who has called for civilian coordination is White House Office of
Science and Technology director Michael Kratsios. "These implications of AI
spread across so many different agencies," he told Fox News, adding that "to
have someone at the White House to be able to work on all those issues across
the agencies is really critical."

No surprise that a White House official wants Trump's AI Force to reside in
the White House; but when it comes to big money and calls of national
security, the military is the colossus, even if the organizational design is
yet unclear.

So, as is often the case with the military, secrecy comes to the rescue. Some
tech leaders are actively asking for their work to be absorbed into the
military's black budget. Guillaume Verdon -- founder and CEO of AI hardware
startup Extropic and a former Google researcher -- argues for locking AI
development safely behind classified doors.

"Any sort of AI Cyberdefense or AI Biodefense work should be a contract from
the US AI Force and under strict clearance/export control, just like any
sensitive defense work," Verdon
[said](https://x.com/beffjezos/status/2101411853356392542?s=20).

Trump muses, and everyone from Silicon Valley tech execs to the Pentagon brass
smells fresh meat, ready to make an AI Force follow their design and their
interests. Concerns about AI itself, the coming AI war, or the future of
humanity are subsumed into an organizational turf war. Meanwhile, secretly,
everyone is eager to siphon off billions and develop secret weapons while the
legislators and the bureaucrats are busy fussing with org charts.

I'm a skeptic of the AI apocalypse narrative (see: "[Is The AI Apocalypse For
Real?](https://www.kenklippenstein.com/p/is-the-ai-apocalypse-for-real)").
However, I do see the dynamic shaping up where some 50-year debate ahead of us
(like the nuclear debate) generates dinners and seminars and conferences and
proposals and guardrails and agreements and treaties. Through all of it, an AI
Force will form and the weapons of our destruction will emerge, with the
people shut out both because it has become a matter of "national security" --
which is to say, none of our business.

Then we'll be asked to enter the contest to design the new AI Force uniform.

Suggestions anyone?
